item.research_question: How do the dual roles of grain boundaries as dislocation obstacles and sources weigh against each other to determine toughness and the brittle-to-ductile transition, and can this explain the minimum in toughness at an intermediate grain size?
item.material_system: Pure tungsten (model material for polycrystalline tungsten)
item.processing_route: Two-dimensional discrete dislocation dynamics modelling; parameters varied: mean free path for dislocation glide (δ), obstacle force (ϕ), and dislocation source spacing (λ); simulations run at 200–800 K with loading rate K˙ = 1 MPa m0.5/s
item.test_conditions: Temperature range 200–800 K; applied stress intensity raised at constant rate; critical stress intensity KIC = 2 MPa m0.5; obstacle force varied from 0.1 to 1000 GPa; source spacing λ varied from 0 to 1000 nm
key_findings: For materials where λ is the mean distance of intrinsic sources and grain boundaries confine the plastic zone, decreasing grain size (decreasing δ) results in decreased toughness.
For materials where λ is the mean distance of grain boundary intersections with the crack front, a simultaneous decrease of δ and λ results in increased toughness.
The positive impact of grain boundaries (as sources) outweighs the negative impact (as obstacles) when λ is dominated by grain boundary intersections.
Toughness passes through a minimum at an intermediate grain size where the relevant measure for λ transitions from intrinsic sources to grain boundary intersections.
The brittle-to-ductile transition temperature passes through a maximum at an intermediate grain size, mirroring the toughness minimum.
In cold-worked metals with elongated grains, increasing the grain aspect ratio increases the anisotropy of fracture toughness.
The derived relationship for grain-size-dependent fracture toughness is K(dδ, dλ) = KIC + kdδ0.5/dλ.
item.mechanism: Grain boundaries act as both obstacles (reducing mean free path δ and promoting pile-ups that suppress dislocation nucleation) and sources (intersection points with the crack front reduce source spacing λ, promoting shielding and blunting). The dominant mechanism depends on grain size: in coarse grains, intrinsic sources dominate (λ constant, δ decreases with grain size, toughness drops); in fine grains, grain boundary intersections dominate (λ decreases with grain size, toughness rises). The transition between these regimes creates a minimum in toughness and a maximum in BDT temperature.
item.limitations: The study uses a two-dimensional model; the BDT temperature determination combines numerical toughness data with experimental yield stress data without fitting, yielding only semi-quantitative results; the model assumes λ and ϕ are independent of temperature.
item.future_work: The authors propose refining the working hypothesis on mechanisms controlling the BDT of pre-deformed, textured, polycrystalline body-centred cubic metals based on the harmonized explanation of contradictory experimental results.
quotes: Our results show that for materials or microstructures for which the mean distance of the intersection points of grain boundaries with the crack front is the relevant measure for λ, a decrease of grain size results in an increase of toughness.
The positive impact of grain boundaries outweighs the negative consequences of dislocation blocking.

The essential point is that relevant measure for λ changes with decreasing grain size from 'the mean distance of the intrinsic sources along the crack front' to 'the mean distance of intersection points of grain boundaries with the crack front'.

item.research_question: To identify the grain-size-dependence of toughness, K=K(d), and the BDT temperature, TBDT=TBDT(d), which was an open question before.
item.processing_route: Two-dimensional discrete dislocation dynamics modelling with parameter studies varying: (i) mean free path for dislocation glide, δ, (ii) obstacle force of the grain boundary, ϕ, and (iii) dislocation source spacing along the crack front, λ.
item.test_conditions: Case study I: varied δ while holding others constant. Case study II: varied λ while holding others constant. Case study III: simultaneously varied δ and λ.
key_findings: A decrease of the mean free path for dislocation glide, δ (a decrease of grain size) results in a decrease of toughness.
A decrease of the dislocation source spacing along the crack front, λ (a decrease of grain size) results in an increase of toughness.
The simultaneous decrease of λ and δ results in an increase of toughness.
Under these test conditions, grain boundaries are always positive, or at least neutral.
Toughness passes through a minimum (and the BDT temperature passes through a maximum) at an intermediate grain size.

The relevant measure for λ changes with decreasing grain size from 'the mean distance of the intrinsic sources along the crack front' to 'the mean distance of intersection points of grain boundaries with the crack front'.
item.mechanism: Grain boundaries act as both obstacles for dislocation glide (reducing toughness) and preferred dislocation nucleation sites at the crack front (increasing toughness). At large grain sizes, intrinsic sources dominate and grain size reduction reduces toughness; at small grain sizes, boundary intersections dominate and grain size reduction increases toughness, creating a minimum in toughness at an intermediate critical grain size.
quotes: The aim of this paper was to identify the grain-size-dependence of toughness, K=K(d), and the BDT temperature, TBDT=TBDT(d), which was an open question before.
The results show, that the simultaneous decrease of λ and δ results in an increase of toughness.

The results of the fundamental case studies presented above, allow a mechanism-based explanation of why toughness passes through a minimum (and the BDT temperature passes through a maximum) at an intermediate grain size.
